intro: Bentivoglio is a small town on the flat farmland of the Po plain, about twenty kilometres north-east of Bologna. In its centre a tall evergreen conifer, about twenty metres high by a reader's measure, rises far above the two-storey buildings around it, its crown a dense dark pyramid that sweeps down to the lawn. A reader sent us its photographs and knows it as a silver fir; we would like to confirm which conifer it is.

question_answer: The Fir of Bentivoglio stands on a lawn beside a building in the centre of Bentivoglio, north-east of Bologna, and can be seen from the street.
question_context: A reader sent us this tree from the centre of Bentivoglio, a town on the flat farmland of the Po plain about twenty kilometres north-east of Bologna, and gave us its coordinates by mail. It is a tall evergreen conifer on a strip of lawn beside a cream two-storey building, with a street lamp and parked cars around it. By the reader's measure it is about twenty metres tall, and its trunk about three metres round. The crown is a dense, dark pyramid whose lower branches sweep almost to the grass, so the trunk is hidden until you stand underneath, where a grey, scaly bole rises straight up and dozens of thin limbs radiate from it. The reader knows it as a silver fir; from the photographs we cannot rule out a spruce, so we list it as a fir and ask readers to confirm. Its age is not known. Its height and girth are the reader's figures, not a register's, and our pin is the point the reader gave us.

trees.story:
A reader sent us this conifer from the centre of Bentivoglio, a small town on the plain north-east of Bologna. "Alto 20 metri circa," they wrote: about twenty metres tall, its trunk about three metres round.

In their photographs it stands on a strip of lawn beside a cream two-storey building, a street lamp and a few parked cars, and it rises far above all of them. The crown is a dense dark pyramid of evergreen branches that sweep down almost to the grass, so thick that the trunk disappears inside it. From underneath the view changes completely. A grey, scaly trunk dotted with old branch scars climbs straight up, and dozens of long, thin limbs spread out from it in every direction like the ribs of an umbrella.

The reader knows it as a silver fir, the fir of the Apennine forests. From the photographs alone we cannot rule out a spruce, so we list it as a fir and ask: if you can tell from its cones or needles, tell us here. Its age is unknown to the reader and to us; if the town has a record of its planting, we would love to see it.

See it first from the street, where the whole pyramid fits in view.

Bark and shoots could also be a spruce, so the genus is stated and the page asks. Access: visible from the street; whether the lawn is public is not confirmed and the access line says so.
